description: Hello! We are a team of 6 passionate individuals dedicated to space technologies, science, and creating innovative solutions. Our current members specialize in software engineering, data science, UI/UX design, and project management. This year at the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are specifically focusing on the Earth Observation and Climate Solutions challenges, aiming to build a high-impact project using NASA's open-source datasets.
summary:
The Enes-tronomers Project is an interactive space-training game that lets players experience what it takes to operate as an astronaut across different environments, from an Earth-based spacecraft to the Moon, Mars, Venus, Europa, Saturn, and deep space.

Instead of only presenting space facts, the project turns them into playable missions. Players manage food, water, oxygen, and radiation while repairing systems, collecting scientific samples, choosing landing sites, responding to space-weather events, and using a virtual laboratory to analyze samples. NASA data and resources are integrated throughout the experience, including information from NASA DONKI, Curiosity RAD, Moon Trek, NASA’s Life Support BVAD, NASA OSDR, and the NASA Image and Video Library.

The goal is to make space science more interactive and accessible, especially for young learners. By combining exploration, problem-solving, resource management, and real scientific information, the project helps players understand that astronaut missions require both scientific knowledge and careful decision-making.
details:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive browser-based space-training experience designed to turn real space science into playable missions.

The player begins by choosing an astronaut and entering a spacecraft where they must learn to manage food, water, oxygen, and radiation. As the mission progresses, they repair spacecraft systems, respond to oxygen emergencies, operate life-support systems, and make decisions about where and how to explore.

The experience then expands beyond the spacecraft. Players can land on the Moon and collect water ice, visit Mars and collect rock and iron samples, explore Venus and collect atmospheric samples, investigate Europa and collect ice cores, interact with Saturn-related missions, and travel into deep space. Scientific samples can be processed in the virtual laboratory, while different environments introduce hazards such as radiation bursts, dust storms, acid gusts, and solar storms.

The project also contains a NASA Data Hub that presents NASA information alongside the gameplay. NASA data is used for space weather, radiation, life-support calculations, lunar landing-site information, scientific images, and spaceflight biology research.

The project was developed as a browser-based application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Canvas-based graphics, SVG illustrations, CSS animations, browser audio APIs, interactive UI components, and external NASA APIs/resources are combined into a single playable experience.

The main creative idea is to make the player learn through consequences rather than simply reading information. For example, oxygen is not just a fact on a screen: the player has to monitor it, repair the relevant system, and make decisions before running out. Similarly, lunar water ice becomes something the player physically searches for, collects, processes, and eventually connects to life-support needs.

The project was designed with accessibility and engagement in mind, including keyboard controls, on-screen controls for touch devices, a reduced-motion mode, high-contrast settings, visual warnings, and clear resource indicators.
